blocks.text: That is, at earliest dawn. Nor does the cockcrow of the night mean anything else in these words of Apuleius at the beginning of book 8: At the cockcrow of the night a certain young man came from the nearest city. And in the Vulgate, Tob. VIII, 11: About the crowing of the cocks Raguel ordered his servants to be summoned; and they went with him to dig a grave. About the crowing of the cocks, that is, at the time when the domestic cocks crow. That the time before daybreak is meant is shown by what is found in verses 13 and 14: And when they had prepared the pit, Raguel returned to his wife and said to her, Send one of your maidservants, and let her see whether he (Tobias) is dead, so that I may bury him before the day grows light. The Hebrew has נקברהו טרם אור הבוקר ואיש לא ידע, We shall bury him before the morning light, so that no one may know. Since, therefore, the same time is sometimes called simply cockcrow, and sometimes more explicitly the second cockcrow, men learned in every field rightly think that by this observation Mark can easily be reconciled with the other Evangelists in specifying the time at which Peter was to deny Christ three times. For according to Mark, Christ foretold to Peter that he would deny him three times πρὶν ἢ δὶς ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι [prin ē dis alektora phōnēsai], before the cock had crowed twice. And indeed, after it had crowed following the first denial, after the third ἐκ δευτέρου ἀλέκτωρ ἐφώνησε [ek deuterou alektōr ephōnēse], the cock crowed again. So Mark has it in ch. 14, verses 30, 68, 69, 70, 71. But in the others the cock does not crow before the third denial. For thus Christ says in Matth. XXVI, 34. Ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ νυκτὶ, πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι, τρὶς ἀπαρνήσῃ με· [En tautē tē nykti, prin alektora phōnēsai, tris aparnēsē me] This night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times. And Luc. XXII, 34. Οὐ μὴ φωνήσει σήμερον ἀλέκτωρ, πρὶν ἢ τρὶς ἀπαρνήσῃ μὴ εἰδέναι με· [Ou mē phōnēsei sēmeron alektōr, prin ē tris aparnēsē mē eidenai me] Today the cock will not crow before you deny three times that you know me. And Ioh. XIII, 38. Οὐ μὴ ἀλέκτωρ φωνήσει, ἕως οὗ ἀπαρνήσῃ με τρίς· [Ou mē alektōr phōnēsei, heōs hou aparnēsē me tris] The cock will not crow before you deny me three times. These seem ἀσύστατα [asystata]. But, they say, they are reconciled without any difficulty if you suppose that Peter first denied about midnight, and that the cock then crowed for the first time; and that he denied the third time about the fourth watch, or about the time usually called cockcrow, and that the cock then crowed again. On this assumption, these words of Christ, The cock will not crow, or Before the cock crows, will be the same as if he had said, Before the time of cockcrow, or The cock will not crow that customary crowing from which the time at which it crows is called ἀλεκτοροφωνία [alektorophōnia], before you have denied me three times. Meanwhile I have no doubt that Mark, who had been a disciple of Peter, reported the very words of Christ, just as he had learned them from Peter. [II, 691] But it sufficed for the others to record what was most important, namely that Christ had not only foreseen and foretold that threefold denial of Peter, but had also specified the time, and that Peter would deny Christ three times before cockcrow. Although it is plain that this is to be understood of the second cockcrow, since this alone is called simply cockcrow, Mark nevertheless expressed it explicitly, and [col. 122] added moreover that Peter's first denial preceded the first cockcrow. But, you will say, between the first and second cockcrow a fourth part of the night usually intervenes; and that span would then have been nearly three hours (for in Judaea, at the season of the year when Christ was delivered to death, the nights are more than eleven hours long); whereas between Peter's first and last denial scarcely half of this span can have elapsed. This is clear from Lucae XXII, 56. 57. 58. For there, when Peter had denied to the maidservant that he knew Christ, which was the first denial, μετὰ βραχὺ [meta brachy], a little later, another, seeing him, said, You too are one of them: but Peter said, Man, I am not; which was the second denial. Καὶ διαστάσης ὡσεὶ ὥϱας μιᾶς [Kai diastasēs hōsei hōras mias], And after about one hour had passed, when another asserted the same thing, Peter denied a third time, and immediately the cock crowed. I answer: 1. The Evangelists reported most things summarily; and while Peter, being accused, tried to clear himself, the matter could have been drawn out at greater length, and, with many words exchanged back and forth, much time could have been spent in the dispute itself. 2. From Luke's words μετὰ βραχὺ [meta brachy] it does not follow that there was no interval of time, or a very short one, between Peter's first and second denial. For John, in chapter 18, from verse 17 to 25, inserts many things as having taken place in that interval. And the third denial, which Luke separates from the second by an interval of about an hour, is nevertheless said in Matthew and Mark to have occurred μετὰ μικρὸν [meta mikron], a little later. Therefore that μετὰ μικρὸν [meta mikron], or, what is the same, μετὰ βραχὺ [meta brachy], can be extended more widely than is thought. 3. Something may be added to Luke's hour, since he did not say precisely that one hour intervened, but ὡσεὶ ὥρας μιᾶς [hōsei hōras mias], about one hour. 4. Although a fourth part of the night usually intervenes between the first and second cockcrow, this is not invariable. For it often happens that cocks crow at random, and not at fixed hours. Scaliger writes in Exercitatio 239 against Cardano that he experienced this both formerly on night watch and later in his nocturnal studies. A cock, therefore, could have anticipated the usual time of cockcrow by one hour after Peter's third denial. Another objection may be raised: when Peter denied Christ, the scribes, priests and elders were in Caiaphas's house to inquire into Christ's life; and Peter meanwhile, having entered the courtyard, waited to see how the matter would finally turn out and what would be decided about Christ. But it is not likely that that assembly lasted so far into the night. For who would believe that so many men from among the leaders of the Jewish people spent almost the whole night without sleep in order to decide this case, when the matter could just as conveniently have been put off to another time? But this objection is raised in vain. For it is certain that it happened so. This will be clear to those who consider [II, 692] how many things were done that night before Peter's third denial. Ὀψίας γενομένης [Opsias genomenēs] ^{a)}, When evening had already come, that is, at the very setting of the sun, Christ celebrated the Passover with the Apostles. He washed their feet ^{b)}. He preached on the occasion ^{c)}. He instituted the eucharistic supper ^{d)}. He restrained with the gravest words the disciples, who were contending among themselves over the primacy ^{e)}. He sang a hymn, which consisted of several Psalms, if the Talmudists are to be believed ^{f)}. He went to the Mount of Olives ^{g)}; and came to an estate named Gethsemane ^{h)}. He withdrew to pray ^{i)}, and after an hour's prayer returned to the disciples; finding them asleep, he rebuked them because they could not keep watch one hour ^{k)}. The same happened a second and a third time ^{l)}. Meanwhile the officers sent with Judas seize Christ ^{m)}. And they lead him first to Annas ^{n)}. And from there to Caiaphas ^{o)}. There the scribes, priests and elders assemble. And Peter, admitted with difficulty into the courtyard and recognized, denies Christ ^{p)}. Christ is questioned by Caiaphas ^{q)}. After this he is denied by Peter a second [col. 123] time ^{r)}, and, after an hour had passed, a third time ^{s)}. No fair judge of the facts will fail to recognize at once that all these things could not have taken place before the dead of night. And it was indeed altogether extraordinary that a man's life should be dealt with at those hours. But, besides the feast that was close at hand, they were driven to it by their savage rage against Christ and by a more than Vatinian hatred with which they were borne against him. Closest to the interpretation we have given comes that of Theophylact on Mark: Ὅπερ δὲ εἶπεν ἀσαφῶς ὁ Ματθαῖος, ὅτι πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι ἡρμήνευσεν ὁ Μάρκος, ὅτι πρὶν φωνῆσαι δίς. Εἰώθασι γὰρ οἱ ἀλέκτορες κατὰ μίαν ἀγωγὴν πολλάκις φωνεῖν, εἶτα οἷον ὑπνώττειν, καὶ πάλιν μετά τινα καιρὸν ἑτέραν ἀρχὴν ποιεῖσθαι τοῦ φωνεῖν· ὃ οὖν εἶπεν ὁ Ματθαῖος, τοῦτό ἐστιν, ὅτι, πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι, τουτέστι, πληρῶσαι τὰς κραυγὰς τῆς πρώτης ἀγωγῆς, ἀπαρνήσῃ με τρίς. [Hoper de eipen asaphōs ho Matthaios, hoti prin alektora phōnēsai hērmēneusen ho Markos, hoti prin phōnēsai dis. Eiōthasi gar hoi alektores kata mian agōgēn pollakis phōnein, eita hoion hypnōttein, kai palin meta tina kairon heteran archēn poieisthai tou phōnein; ho oun eipen ho Matthaios, touto estin, hoti, prin alektora phōnēsai, toutesti, plērōsai tas kraugas tēs prōtēs agōgēs, aparnēsē me tris.] What Matthew says obscurely, „Before the cock crows“, Mark has explained as before it crows twice. For cocks are accustomed often to crow in one stretch, then, as it were, to sleep, and after some time to begin crowing again. What Matthew said, then, namely, before the cock crows, means: before it completes the cry of the first crowing, you will deny me three times ^{(1)}.
